prompt: Write an essay of advice for a new PhD student on choosing a research problem. About 800 words. Output only the essay, with no title.
raw:
Choosing a research problem is the first real act of scholarship you will perform, and it is easy to treat it as a hunt for a topic that will impress a committee. It is better treated as a decision about how you will spend several years of attention. The problem you choose will determine whom you talk to, what you read before breakfast, which failures you can tolerate, and whether the work still feels worth doing when the first paper is rejected. Taste, fit, and feasibility matter more than novelty announced in the abstract.

Start with what you can sustain. Curiosity that survives contact with the literature is rarer than curiosity that flares in a seminar. Notice which papers you reread without being assigned them, which arguments you want to repair rather than merely cite, and which puzzles return after you have tried to set them aside. A problem that merely sounds important will not carry you through the months when the methods are dull and the results are ambiguous. Importance can be learned; endurance has to be partly already there.

Read enough to know the neighborhood, but do not wait for a complete map. New students often postpone commitment until they feel they have surveyed the field. That survey never ends, and the delay teaches avoidance rather than judgment. Read the recent reviews, the canonical papers, and a handful of current articles that disagree with one another. Then write, in a page or two, what is actually unsettled. If you cannot say what would count as progress, you do not yet have a problem; you have a theme. A theme can organize a reading list. A problem organizes an inquiry: it has a question, a reason the question is open, and a plausible way of getting leverage on it.

Leverage is the part students underestimate. A good problem is not merely unanswered; it is answerable with the tools, data, time, and collaborators you can realistically assemble. Ask what a first result would look like in eighteen months, not what a definitive theory would look like in a decade. Small, sharp questions often open larger ones; grandiose questions often collapse into vague literature reviews. Prefer a problem where a negative result would still teach you something. If the only interesting outcome is confirmation of a hoped-for effect, you have designed a bet rather than a project.

Talk to people who have finished the kind of work you imagine doing. Advisors know the local constraints: funding cycles, equipment, data access, the temperament of examiners, the habits of journals. Peers a year or two ahead know the hidden costs: which techniques take a semester to learn, which datasets are messier than their papers admit, which collaborations require diplomacy you do not yet have. Listen for warnings about scope. A problem that requires three new methods, a new dataset, and a new theoretical framework is usually three problems wearing a single title. Choose one hard thing and keep the rest as ordinary as you can.

Be wary of fashion, but do not confuse obscurity with integrity. Fields have moments when money, conferences, and citation counts converge on a narrow set of questions. Some of those questions are genuinely ripe; some are crowded because they are easy to publish. Enter a crowded area only if you can see a distinction that is not merely a new dataset or a slightly different model. Enter a neglected area only if you can explain, to a skeptical reader, why neglect was a mistake rather than a signal that the ground is barren. Obscurity does not confer depth, and popularity does not confer shallowness.

Consider the audience you want to join. Research problems are social objects. They live in communities with standards of evidence, preferred methods, and unspoken taboos. You do not have to adopt every convention, but you should know which ones you are challenging and why. If your problem sits between fields, identify at least one community that would recognize a successful answer as its own business. Interdisciplinary work fails less often from lack of vision than from lack of a home: no one feels obliged to read it, fund it, or teach it. A bridge needs footings on both banks.

Protect your ability to change your mind without treating every doubt as a verdict. Early commitment should be provisional. Set a date by which you will have a concrete plan, a pilot, or a clear reason to switch. Switching is not failure if it is informed; drifting is. Write down the assumptions your problem depends on, and revisit them when evidence arrives. Many students cling to a question because they have already invested months in it. Sunk costs are not arguments. The relevant question is whether the next year of work is the best use of the skills you now have, not whether the last year was wasted.

Attend to ethics and access early, not as an afterthought. If your problem involves people, animals, sensitive data, or communities that have been studied extractively before, the constraints are part of the problem, not paperwork surrounding it. A design that cannot be done responsibly cannot be done. Similarly, if the work depends on proprietary data, a single gatekeeper, or instruments you do not control, ask what happens if access narrows. Robust problems have more than one path to evidence.

Finally, choose a problem that leaves you more capable than it found you. The dissertation is a product, but the PhD is an apprenticeship in judgment. A problem that teaches you how to frame questions, handle evidence, and write for a critical reader will serve you even if the particular finding is modest. Seek work that is hard in a way you can get better at: hard because the reasoning is subtle, the measurement is careful, or the writing must be exact, not hard only because the scope is inflated. When you can explain your problem to an intelligent outsider in a few calm sentences, say why it matters without borrowing the language of a grant advertisement, and describe the next concrete step, you are ready to begin. The rest is iteration, and iteration is the job.
